title: Iodine Uptake and Diffusion Evaluation in Sheep and Pig Meniscus Tissue
author: Orellana, Parrilli
materials:
Timing: variable
1.Prepare the Formaldehyde fixative.a.Prepare a 4% formaldehyde solution in Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 6.9) can be prepared freshly from paraformaldehyde or used as a commercially available buffered formaldehyde solution (see key resources table).b.Store the fixative at 4°C for up to one month and prepare fresh if any precipitation or yellow discoloration occurs.
CRITICAL: Ensure that the fixative solution is handled under a fume hood with proper personal protective equipment to prevent exposure to hazardous chemicals.
Note: This protocol was developed using formaldehyde as fixative. Other fixatives can be used; however, they could affect iodine binding and diffusion, and should be validated accordingly.
2.Prepare the PBS solution.a.Dissolve 1 tablet of PBS (see the key resources table) in 200 mL of distilled water. The resulting solution will have a pH of approximately 7.2–7.6.b.Store at 4°C for up to 1 month.
CRITICAL: Ensure the solution remains clear and free of contamination.
3.Prepare the Water-based Lugol’s Iodine Solution.a.Prepare an aqueous 1.25% w/v of I2 and 2.5% w/v of KI solution using a stirring instrument.b.Store in a light-protected container at 4°C for up to 1 month.
CRITICAL: Handle iodine and potassium iodide powders inside a fume hood to prevent inhalation. Avoid contact with metal surfaces to minimize corrosion risk; use non-metallic tools and containers when possible.
Note: If stored, stir the solution again for a few minutes before use to resuspend any settled iodine.
Note: Iodine-based contrast agents are the focus of this protocol. While other contrast agents can be used, their diffusion dynamics may differ, requiring optimization of concentration and staining duration.
4.Prepare the PBS-based Lugol’s Iodine Solution.a.Prepare a PBS-based 1.25% w/v of I2 and 2.5% w/v of KI solution.b.Store in a light-protected container at 4°C for up to 1 month.
CRITICAL: Handle iodine and potassium iodide powders inside a fume hood to prevent inhalation. Avoid contact with metal surfaces to minimize corrosion risk; use non-metallic tools and containers when possible.
Note: If stored, stir the solution again for a few minutes before use to resuspend any settled iodine.

steps.title: Prepare 4% formaldehyde fixative
steps.instruction: Make a 4% (w/v) formaldehyde solution in phosphate‑buffered saline (PBS, pH 6.9) either by diluting paraformaldehyde or using a commercial buffered formaldehyde; store the solution at 4 °C for up to one month and prepare fresh if any precipitation or yellow discoloration appears. Handle under a fume hood with appropriate PPE.

steps.title: Prepare PBS buffer solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve one tablet of PBS in 200 mL of distilled water to obtain a buffer with pH approximately 7.2–7.6; store at 4 °C for up to one month. Ensure the solution remains clear and free of contamination.

steps.title: Prepare water‑based Lugol’s iodine solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve iodine (I₂) to a final concentration of 1.25 % w/v and potassium iodide (KI) to 2.5 % w/v in distilled water while stirring; store the solution in a light‑protected container at 4 °C for up to one month. Handle iodine and KI powders inside a fume hood, avoid metal tools, and stir the solution for a few minutes before each use to resuspend any settled iodine.

steps.title: Prepare PBS‑based Lugol’s iodine solution
steps.instruction: Prepare a PBS‑based solution containing 1.25 % w/v I₂ and 2.5 % w/v KI using the same procedure as the water‑based solution; store in a light‑protected container at 4 °C for up to one month, handling powders in a fume hood and avoiding metal contact. Stir briefly before use if stored.

steps.title: Fix meniscal samples
steps.instruction: Immerse each meniscus in 4 % formaldehyde fixative for 24 hours at room temperature.

steps.title: Wash meniscal samples
steps.instruction: Wash the fixed menisci three times with either distilled water or PBS, using approximately 100 mL for each wash, according to the subsequent staining solution to be used.

steps.title: Stain menisci in iodine solution
steps.instruction: Place each meniscus in ~100 mL of the appropriate Lugol’s iodine solution (water‑based for 6 sheep and 6 pig menisci; PBS‑based for 6 pig menisci) and incubate for up to 24 days at 22 °C–25 °C under static conditions.

steps.title: Collect staining solution aliquots
steps.instruction: At days 0, 1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24, withdraw 1 mL of the staining solution from each sample and transfer into labeled Eppendorf tubes.

steps.title: Store aliquots for downstream analysis
steps.instruction: Keep all collected 1 mL aliquots at 4 °C until they are processed for micro‑CT imaging, UV‑Vis spectroscopy, and pH measurements.

steps.title: Process micro‑CT data
steps.instruction: Analyze the CT datasets using Fiji and Avizo as follows:

substeps.instruction: Open each dataset in Fiji; apply the IsoData algorithm to segment meniscal tissue (do not use a global threshold). Verify segmentation manually.
Normalize segmented volumes to the original day‑0 volume for each sample; set day‑0 volume as 100 % and calculate volume reduction at later time points.
In Avizo, segment the meniscus using a threshold range from the IsoData value up to the maximum grayscale value (65535 for 16‑bit images) and measure volume with the Volume Fraction tool.
Create 3‑D renderings using Maximum Intensity Projection and average 150 consecutive radial slices per time point.
Convert the original 16‑bit CT images to 8‑bit (input range 0–65535, output range 0–255) using the Convert Image Type module.
Measure the linear attenuation coefficient (μ) for each time point with the Label Analysis module.
Calculate Hounsfield Units (HU) using HU = ((μ_tissue – μ_water) / (μ_water – μ_air)) × 1000; obtain μ_water by scanning 1 mL of water under identical CT settings.

In MATLAB, define a region of interest extending from the outer periphery to the inner region with a fixed height of 0.25 mm and a radial width appropriate for the species; average values from 100 central radial CT slices.

Run the provided MATLAB script: select the main folder, set commonHeight = 400 slices, commonWidth = 10 voxels, fileNames = {'day0','day1','day4','day8','day12','day16','day20','day24'}, input GL_air = 0, enter GL_water (water phantom gray level), compute HU for each image, determine the global maximum HU, calculate normalized iodine concentration ((HU‑HU_day0_mean)/(HU_max‑HU_day0_mean)×100), and store profiles.
Average concentration profiles across all subjects, plot a heatmap of depth (0 = outer edge, 1 = inner edge) versus time, and save results as a .mat file and as a CSV table.

steps.title: Perform UV‑Vis spectroscopy of staining solutions
steps.instruction: Quantify iodine species in the collected aliquots as follows:

substeps.instruction: Dilute each aliquot 500‑fold to obtain a baseline spectrum of the solution.
For I⁻ detection (peak at 228 nm), further dilute the sample 3 000‑fold and record the absorbance at 228 nm.
For I₃⁻ detection (peaks at 288 nm and 351 nm), dilute the sample 500‑fold and record absorbance at 288 nm and 351 nm.
Analyze water‑based and PBS‑based iodine solutions specifically at days 0, 1, and 24; record a solvent (water or PBS) baseline as a blank before each measurement.

steps.title: Measure pH of iodine solutions
steps.instruction: Using a calibrated pH meter, measure the pH of both the water‑based and PBS‑based Lugol’s iodine solutions at days 0, 1, and 24; record the values for each time point.

description: Here, we describe the procedures used to evaluate iodine uptake and diffusion in sheep and pig meniscal tissues using contrast-enhanced micro-CT and UV-Vis spectroscopy, as applied in our associated research study.1 This protocol assesses iodine distribution in soft tissues over time using sequential micro-CT imaging after iodine staining. Although this protocol focuses on meniscal tissue from sheep and pigs, similar approaches can be used for other soft tissues or animal models that require diffusion-based contrast analysis.
